title: Credibility assessment of fluid–structure interaction models for aortic valve leaflet coaptation and stress under three physiologic mechanisms
runhead: Aortic valve FSI credibility under V&V 40

models.name: A-LEAF (Arbitrary Lagrangian–Eulerian FSI)
models.what_it_computes: Transient coaptation area fraction and maximum principal stress on leaflets using ALE Navier–Stokes coupled to anisotropic hyperelastic shells

models.name: E-VALVE (Embedded-boundary FSI)
models.what_it_computes: Leaflet coaptation metric and peak principal stress using an immersed-boundary flow solver coupled to thin-shell finite elements

models.name: PULSE (Partitioned ROM–CFD–FEM)
models.what_it_computes: Coaptation area fraction and peak leaflet stress via a partitioned solver coupling a reduced-order inflow circuit, incompressible CFD, and nonlinear shells

mechanisms.name: Diastolic sealing
mechanisms.why_it_matters: Sustained coaptation under physiologic afterload prevents regurgitation; stresses during closure influence durability.

mechanisms.name: Peak systolic opening
mechanisms.why_it_matters: High flow rates and leaflet curvature determine stress levels linked to fatigue and material damage.

mechanisms.name: Rapid closure water-hammer
mechanisms.why_it_matters: Transient pressure reversal during deceleration produces short-duration stress spikes associated with early tears.

deviation.detail: Throughout, the 'Model inputs' credibility factor is referred to as the 'Input Realism Index (IRI)' and scored under that name.

sections: Question of Interest and Context of Use (COU): Use three FSI models to predict leaflet coaptation area fraction and peak principal stress under diastolic sealing, peak systolic opening, and rapid closure; compare against pulse-duplicator measurements for a baseline valve to establish trust; then apply the validated framework to rank candidate leaflet designs without additional bench tests for all three mechanisms.

Model Risk Analysis (ASME V&V 40): Model influence High because simulation results are the primary evidence for design acceptance or down-selection; decision consequence High because incorrect predictions could lead to inadequate coaptation or elevated leaflet stress with patient harm; overall model risk High, warranting stringent evidence across the specified credibility factors.

Computational Models and Implementation Notes: Governing equations, coupling strategies, constitutive laws for leaflet tissue, fluid properties, numerical libraries and version control noted where relevant.

Mechanisms of Interest and Associated Test Conditions: Definition of load cases, flow/pressure waveforms, and valve mounting geometry mapped to in vitro pulse-duplicator setups for diastole, peak systole, and rapid closure.
Physical Test Samples: Description of manufactured valve specimens, leaflet materials, and mounting fixtures used for bench measurements that serve as comparators.

Credibility Plan and Scoring Approach: For each model × mechanism pair, levels will be assigned for Discretization error, Model form, Input Realism Index (IRI), Numerical solver error, Test conditions, Test samples; scoring will follow standard gradations with pre-defined acceptance targets for coaptation and stress.

Verification Methods: Mesh/time-step refinement studies for Discretization error; iterative and coupling tolerance studies for Numerical solver error, including convergence diagnostics for all three mechanisms.

Validation Methods: Model form assessment via comparison of predicted coaptation geometry and stress patterns to measurements; Input Realism Index (IRI) assessment via traceability of boundary drivings and material parameters to test-derived values; alignment of Test conditions and Test samples between simulations and bench setups for each mechanism.

Credibility Results: Per-factor scores for each model × mechanism pair with justification, covering Discretization error, Model form, Input Realism Index (IRI), Numerical solver error, Test conditions, and Test samples.

Discussion: How credibility outcomes support or limit the use of each model for coaptation and stress decisions within the COU; implications for design ranking and evidence sufficiency given High model risk.
